topics.name: Registration, layers and change of control

items.q: A borrower clears the overdue on the loan that turned NPA but is still behind on another facility. Can the account be upgraded?
items.a:
No. Asset classification is **borrower-wise, not facility-wise**: once one facility is an NPA, every facility to that borrower, and any securities the NBFC holds of that borrower, is NPA too. An NPA can be upgraded to standard only when the borrower pays the **entire arrears of interest and principal on all facilities**.

Overdue, SMA and NPA status are set in the day-end process for the relevant date, whatever time that process actually runs, and the SMA or NPA date is the calendar date it is run for.

items.q: Under a co-lending arrangement, if the partner lender classifies the borrower as SMA or NPA, does the NBFC have to follow?
items.a:
Yes. Co-lent exposures follow **borrower-level classification across both lenders**. If either lender classifies its share as SMA or NPA because of a default under the arrangement, the other lender must apply the same classification to its share. The lenders must share this information close to real time, and no later than the end of the next working day.

The NBFC must keep at least **10 per cent** of each loan on its own books. As originator, it may give a default loss guarantee of up to **5 per cent** of the loans outstanding under the arrangement. Selling a co-lent loan to a third party needs the consent of both lenders.

These rules cover arrangements entered into from 1 January 2026, or from an earlier date the NBFC adopted in its policy. Arrangements made before that date stay under the earlier rules.

refs.label: Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk Directions para 124

items.q: How does a default loss guarantee (DLG) affect the NBFC's asset classification, and how large can it be?
items.a:
It does not change it. The NBFC classifies and provisions each underlying loan under the IRACP Directions as if there were no DLG. The amount invoked is not set off against the individual loans, so each borrower still owes the full amount.

The DLG cover on a portfolio cannot exceed **5 per cent of the amount disbursed** from that portfolio. For an implicit guarantee, the provider cannot bear performance risk above the equivalent of 5 per cent. The NBFC must invoke the DLG within **120 days of overdue**, unless the borrower pays before then. The DLG must stay in force for at least the longest tenor of any loan in the portfolio. The cover can be cash, a fixed deposit with a scheduled commercial bank under lien, or a bank guarantee.

The covered portfolio (the DLG set) is fixed when the arrangement starts and cannot be topped up with new loans. Once invoked, DLG cover cannot be reinstated, even from later recoveries.

items.q: Can an NBFC enter into a compromise settlement with a borrower classified as a wilful defaulter or fraud?
items.a:
Yes. The settlement does not affect any criminal proceedings already under way, and the penal measures for frauds and wilful defaulters continue to apply. Settlement is never the borrower's right; it is the NBFC's commercial decision, and every settlement with a fraud or wilful defaulter needs **Board approval**. No official who sanctioned the loan can take part in approving its settlement. Three rules decide how it is treated:

1. A settlement whose payment period runs **beyond three months** is treated as a **restructuring**. So is any part settlement, and so is any future contingent recovery that is recognised on the balance sheet.
2. The NBFC cannot take a fresh exposure to a borrower it has settled with until a cooling period has passed. The board sets this period, but it must be at least **12 months**.
3. If a recovery case is pending before a court or tribunal, the settlement needs a **consent decree** from that forum.

A partial technical write-off does not reset provisioning. Provisioning and asset classification are still worked out on the original exposure.

refs.label: Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions para 97

items.q: Can an NBFC charge a pre-payment penalty on a floating rate business loan to an MSE?
items.a:
It depends on the NBFC's layer and the loan size, for loans sanctioned or renewed from **1 January 2026**:

- An **Upper Layer** NBFC cannot levy pre-payment charges on any floating rate business loan to an individual or a micro or small enterprise.
- A **Middle Layer** NBFC cannot levy them where the sanctioned amount or limit is **up to ₹50 lakh**.
- In other cases, charges follow the NBFC's board-approved policy. On a term loan, they must be based on the amount prepaid; on a cash credit or overdraft, on no more than the sanctioned limit, and nothing at all if the borrower gives notice of non-renewal and the facility closes on its due date.

Floating rate loans to individuals for non-business purposes carry no pre-payment charge at all. These rules apply whatever the source of funds and with no lock-in period. No charge can be levied unless it was disclosed in the sanction letter and the loan agreement, and in the Key Facts Statement where one is required. No charge can be levied at all where the NBFC itself caused the pre-payment.

items.q: What retention does an NBFC need when it securitises loans, and what does not count towards it?
How do concentration limits differ for a Middle Layer and an Upper Layer NBFC?
items.a:
**Middle Layer:** exposure, counting credit and investment together, cannot exceed **25 per cent of Tier 1 capital** to a single party or **40 per cent** to a single group. These can go up by 5 and 10 percentage points respectively if the extra exposure is to infrastructure. NBFC-IFCs have their own limits of 30 and 50 per cent.

**Upper Layer:** the Large Exposures Framework applies instead. The single counterparty limit is **20 per cent of the eligible capital base**. The board can allow 5 per cent more under a board policy, with the exceptional reasons recorded in writing, and a further 5 per cent of Tier 1 is allowed for infrastructure, but the limit can never exceed **25 per cent** (**30 per cent** for an NBFC-IFC). The group limit is **25 per cent**, plus 10 per cent of Tier 1 for infrastructure; an NBFC-IFC can go 20 per cent of Tier 1 higher for a group. Exposure includes off-balance sheet items.

items.q: What are the rules for bullet repayment gold loans?
items.a:
A consumption loan against gold or silver repaid as a bullet can run for **at most 12 months**. It can then be renewed on the borrower's formal request and after a fresh credit assessment, but only after the borrower pays the accrued interest, only within the permitted LTV, and only if the loan is standard.

For a bullet loan, the LTV and the loan amount are measured on the **total amount repayable at maturity**, not the amount disbursed. The same maturity amount decides whether a detailed assessment of repayment capacity is needed (above ₹2.5 lakh of total lending to the borrower against eligible collateral). Renewals and top-ups must be identifiable in the NBFC's core system.

items.q: When does an NBFC need RBI's prior approval for a change in shareholding or control?
items.a:
Prior written permission of RBI is needed for:

1. any takeover or acquisition of control, whether or not management changes; and
2. any change in shareholding, including gradual increases, that results in acquiring or transferring **26 per cent or more** of the paid-up equity capital.

Crossing 26 per cent only because of a court-approved buyback or capital reduction needs no prior approval, but must be reported within one month. Deposit-taking HFCs have a separate 10 per cent test for foreign investors.

Separately, a change in management that replaces **more than 30 per cent of the directors** (not counting independent directors) also needs RBI's prior written permission. Directors re-elected on retirement by rotation do not count.

refs.label: Acquisition of Shareholding or Control Directions para 6

items.q: Can an NBFC charge penal interest on a loan?
items.a:
No. A penalty for breaking the material terms of a loan must be a **penal charge**, not penal interest added to the rate of interest. Penal charges cannot be capitalised: no interest is charged on them, and a fresh penal charge cannot be levied on earlier penal charges. Penal charges must be reasonable, commensurate with the breach, levied only on the amount in default, and set under a board-approved policy.

This applies to loans taken from 1 April 2024, and to older loans from 30 June 2024. It does not apply to credit cards, ECBs, trade credits, structured obligations covered by product-specific directions, or other foreign currency loans.

items.q: Does my NBFC need an Internal Ombudsman?
items.a:
Yes, if on 31 March 2025 it was a deposit-taking NBFC with **10 or more branches**, or a non-deposit-taking NBFC with assets of **₹5,000 crore or more** and a public customer interface. An NBFC that meets these tests later must comply within six months of meeting them.

HFCs, CICs, IDF-NBFCs, NBFC-IFCs, NOFHCs, primary dealers and mortgage guarantee companies are outside these Directions, as are NBFCs in insolvency, liquidation or under RBI directions.

items.q: A cyber incident hits a group that has an NBFC, a stock broker and an insurance broker. Who does each entity notify, and by when?
items.a:
Each entity runs its own **six-hour** clock, and each also reports to CERT-In.

- **NBFC:** report on RBI's DAKSH portal within **six hours of detection**. This applies to every Middle and Upper Layer NBFC and to Base Layer NBFCs with assets of ₹500 crore or more. An **HFC reports to NHB** instead of RBI. The NBFC must also notify CERT-In proactively.
- **SEBI-regulated entity (stock broker, depository participant and others):** incidents covered by the CERT-In Directions go to SEBI and CERT-In within **6 hours** of noticing them or being told of them. SEBI is told by email at mkt_incidents@sebi.gov.in within 6 hours, and the details go on SEBI's Incident Reporting Portal within **24 hours**. A stock broker or DP also reports to the stock exchange or depository within the same 6 hours.
- **IRDAI-regulated entity:** report to IRDAI in the prescribed format within **6 hours** of noticing the incident or being told of it.
- **Every entity:** CERT-In's Directions of 28 April 2022 require the listed incident types, including ransomware, data breaches and unauthorised access, to be reported to CERT-In within **6 hours** of noticing them or being told of them. This covers a small Base Layer NBFC too, even though RBI sets it no DAKSH deadline.

The clock starts when the incident is noticed, not when its cause is confirmed. If personal data is involved, the data breach duties under the DPDP Act apply as well, from 13 May 2027.

items.q: Customer data leaks through a collection agency the NBFC uses. Whose breach is it, and what must be reported?
items.a:
It is the **NBFC's** breach. Outsourcing does not reduce the NBFC's obligations, and it is responsible for the actions of its service providers, including recovery agents.

- **RBI, now:** the NBFC must **immediately notify RBI** of a security breach or leak of confidential customer information, and it is **liable to its customers** for any damage. This applies to material outsourcing at every layer, including recovery work.
- **IT vendors (Middle and Upper Layer):** where an NBFC in these layers materially outsources IT services, the six-hour reporting to RBI runs from **detection by the service provider**, not from when the NBFC hears of it. The contract must make the vendor report without delay.
- **DPDP, from 13 May 2027:** the NBFC as Data Fiduciary remains responsible for processing done for it by a Data Processor. On becoming aware of a personal data breach it must tell **each affected customer** without delay (what happened, the likely consequences, what is being done, what the customer can do, and a contact person). It must tell the **Data Protection Board** without delay, and send a detailed report within **72 hours** of becoming aware, unless the Board allows longer on a written request.

items.q: A forensic audit flags a borrower account. What must happen before it is classified as fraud, and what is due after?
items.a:
**Before classification:** the NBFC must follow natural justice. Each person or entity it proposes to classify as fraudulent gets a detailed show cause notice and at least **21 days** to reply. This can include the borrower, its promoters and whole-time directors, and third parties such as valuers, chartered accountants and advocates, where fraud is alleged against them. It then serves a **reasoned order**. This applies even where a law enforcement agency has already started investigating on its own.

**After classification:**
- report the fraud **immediately** to the police or other law enforcement agency;
- file the **Fraud Monitoring Return** with RBI within **14 days** of classification, whatever the amount (an HFC reports to NHB);
- have the accounts of group companies with a common promoter or whole-time director examined.

Robbery, theft, burglary and dacoity follow a separate route: an email to RBI's Fraud Monitoring Group within **seven days** of the event, and a quarterly return within **15 days** of the quarter end.

These Directions apply to Upper and Middle Layer NBFCs and to Base Layer NBFCs with assets of ₹500 crore or more.

items.q: The Principal Officer suspects a transaction. When must the STR be filed, and can the account be frozen meanwhile?
items.a:
File the **Suspicious Transaction Report** with FIU-IND within **seven working days** of being satisfied that the transaction is suspicious. Cash Transaction Reports for a month are due by the **15th of the next month**. Each day of delay in reporting, or in correcting a wrongly reported transaction, counts as a **separate violation**.

The NBFC must **not restrict operations** in the account just because it filed an STR. If it suspects money laundering or terrorist financing and believes that carrying out customer due diligence would tip off the customer, it may stop the due diligence and must file an STR instead. The STR itself must be kept confidential.

items.q: A customer's KYC update is overdue. What must the NBFC have done?
items.a:
**Periodicity:** at least once every **2 years** for high-risk customers, **8 years** for medium risk and **10 years** for low risk, counted from account opening or the last update.

**Notices:** before the due date, at least **three advance intimations**, one of them by letter. After the due date, at least **three reminders**, one of them by letter.

**Low-risk individuals:** the NBFC must allow all transactions and get the KYC updated within **one year** of it falling due (or by 30 June 2026, if that was later), with the account under regular monitoring.

**What counts as an update (individuals):** if nothing has changed, a self-declaration through the registered email, registered mobile, the app or a letter is enough. If only the address has changed, a self-declaration of the new address is enough, with the NBFC verifying it within two months. If the documents on file have expired, the NBFC must do full KYC as for a new customer, and it verifies PAN with the issuing authority where available.

**Customers other than individuals:** a self-declaration of no change must come through an authorised official or a board resolution, and the NBFC must check that its beneficial ownership details are still accurate.

The NBFC cannot reject an update request without recording its reasons.

items.q: A borrower has repaid a home loan in full. When must the property documents go back, and what if they are late or lost?
items.a:
The NBFC must release all original property documents and remove any registered charge within **30 days** of full repayment or settlement. The borrower chooses where to collect them: the branch that serviced the loan or any other office holding them.

If release or charge removal goes beyond 30 days, the NBFC must tell the borrower why. If the delay is the NBFC's fault, it pays the borrower **₹5,000 for each day** of delay. If documents are lost or damaged, the NBFC must help get certified copies and bear the cost. It gets **30 more days** for this, so compensation runs only after **60 days** in total.

The sanction letter must state where and when the documents will be returned. The NBFC must publish its procedure for returning documents to legal heirs when a borrower dies.

Pledged gold or silver follows a shorter clock: it must be returned the **same day**, and in any case within **seven working days** of full repayment, with the same ₹5,000 a day compensation for delay.

items.q: A borrower complains that their credit report still shows an overdue they cleared. What is the deadline, and who pays if it is missed?
items.a:
The complaint must be resolved within **30 calendar days** of the borrower first filing it with the lender or the credit bureau. After that, the borrower gets **₹100 for each calendar day** of delay.

Where the complaint is filed with the credit bureau, the lender has at most **21 days** to resolve its part and confirm to the bureau, and the bureau has the rest of the 30. The compensation is split between them in proportion to the delay each caused. The complaint counts as resolved on the date the corrected credit report is sent to the borrower.

The lender must also send an SMS or email alert to the borrower when it reports a default or days past due to a credit bureau.

items.q: An NBFC with listed debt misses a payment on a bank loan. When must it tell the stock exchange?
items.a:
It depends on what was missed:

- **Loan from a bank or financial institution** (including cash credit): if the default continues beyond **30 days**, disclose promptly and within **24 hours from the 30th day**.
- **Unlisted NCDs or NCRPS:** disclose promptly and within **24 hours of the default**.
- **Listed NCDs or NCRPS:** follow the listed debt rules under the Listing Regulations.

A default means not paying interest or principal in full on the due date. For cash credit and other revolving facilities, it means the outstanding stays above the sanctioned limit or drawing power, whichever is lower, for more than 30 days. The entity must also make a quarterly disclosure of loans in default beyond 30 days and of unlisted debt securities in default.

refs.label: SEBI Master Circular for non-convertible securities, Chapter V

items.q: A policyholder is in hospital on a cashless health policy. How fast must the insurer act?
items.a:
- **Cashless authorisation:** decide immediately, and within **one hour** of receiving the request.
- **Final authorisation at discharge:** within **three hours** of the hospital's request. The policyholder must not be made to wait to be discharged. If the insurer takes longer than three hours, it bears any extra amount the hospital charges.

refs.label: IRDAI Master Circular on Health Insurance Business
